**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination / Technical and Vocational Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Religious Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

À faire relire par un spécialiste des études religieuses avant mise en avant.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent can Saul not be held responsible for his failures as king in Israel?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Saul, anointed by Samuel as the first king of Israel (1 Samuel 9-10), began well but ended his reign rejected by God and killed on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31). The question asks how far circumstances and other people, rather than Saul himself, account for his failures.

**1. Arguments that Saul was responsible.**
(i) *Disobedience at Gilgal (1 Samuel 13).* Faced with Philistine pressure and a deserting army, Saul did not wait for Samuel and offered the burnt offering himself, thereby taking over a priestly function. Samuel told him that his kingdom would not continue.
(ii) *Disobedience in the war against the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15).* Saul was ordered to destroy Amalek, but he spared King Agag and the best of the animals. When confronted, he put the blame on the people and said he wanted to make sacrifice. Samuel replied that obedience is better than sacrifice, and Saul was rejected.
(iii) *Rash decisions and cruelty.* The oath that forbade the people to eat before evening (1 Samuel 14) harmed his army and nearly cost the life of his son Jonathan. After David's success he grew jealous and repeatedly tried to kill him (1 Samuel 18-20, 23-24), and he had the priests of Nob massacred for helping David (1 Samuel 22).
(iv) *Consulting a medium.* Although he had expelled mediums from the land, before his last battle he consulted the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28), which was forbidden.
(v) *Admissions.* On several occasions Saul himself confessed, "I have sinned" (1 Samuel 15, 24, 26), which suggests that he accepted a measure of responsibility.

**2. Arguments that other factors reduce his responsibility.**
(i) *Difficult circumstances.* Saul became king at a time of Philistine domination, with no standing army, no capital and no administrative system, and a loosely united tribal society. In 1 Samuel 13 his men were scattering in fear and Samuel was late, so his action at Gilgal, though wrong, was understandable.
(ii) *The attitude of Samuel.* Samuel was reluctant about kingship from the start (1 Samuel 8, 12), seeing it as a rejection of God, and he did not give Saul the support of a prophet-adviser. Samuel's strictness and his announcement of rejection so early may have undermined Saul. Samuel anointed David in private (1 Samuel 16), so that a rival chosen by God was growing up in Saul's own court.
(iii) *Divine rejection and the "evil spirit".* The narrative says that the spirit of the Lord left Saul and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him (1 Samuel 16:14). On this view his depression, jealousy and rages were not entirely under his control. Some modern readers see here a mental illness.
(iv) *Pressure from the people.* In 1 Samuel 15 Saul said he had yielded to the people who wanted to keep the animals.
(v) *A tragic figure.* Saul's courage in the last battle, his victories over Ammon (1 Samuel 11) and others, and his loyalty to the people show that he was not a wholly bad ruler.

**3. Evaluation.** The textual evidence suggests that Saul bears most of the responsibility for the clear acts of disobedience (Gilgal, Amalek), his jealousy and the massacre at Nob, and for turning to the medium. The circumstances, the harshness of Samuel's judgement and the effect of the spirit of torment lessen but do not remove his guilt, as the writer stresses that obedience was demanded of a king.

**Conclusion.** Saul can be excused only to a limited extent: the Philistine crisis, the lack of structures, Samuel's role and his mental torment explain much, but his repeated disobedience, jealousy and violence were his own choices. The tradition therefore judges him as largely responsible for his failures, while recognising the tragedy of his reign.
